The “matter of intellect” here means imaginal forms, in line with the author's own account. The “matter of soul” means sensible forms. Each is called matter because it is joined to its form, changes into it, and becomes it.
This refers to the wonders that the images of the intellectual world contain.

This means that each being longs for a real inner union with its source, and for direct knowledge of it. This is the state the author elsewhere calls “all things in all things,” since no veil separates beings beyond matter. The commentator reads the desire to rise in this way because fully complete beings do not feel lack or longing. The passage also concerns the intellects of rising human souls, as the author's next words show.

These forms are not dark and made of matter. They exist more completely and clearly than physical forms. Nor are they merely imaginary; they can be seen. To be seen means to take a form that the shared sense can perceive, whether that form comes from inside or outside. The outward senses are only pathways that lead to this shared power of perception, like five rivers flowing into one pool.

The proof that the visible world reveals these hidden forms is that natural processes ripen bodies and plants and change them. Nature itself is like a fire with three flames. Imagine what happens when it changes and appears in another world, with its chains, shackles, scorpions, and snakes.

Matter, decay, and passing away belong only to this world. If their features were carried into another world, there would not be more than one kind of world. In brief, fully formed beings return to intellect; extended things that hold together or flow away return to the pit of matter; and matter returns to destruction, because lack rules over it. As we said earlier, powers and unrealized possibilities return to matter, while complete forms return to the source of complete forms. This does not contradict the truth that all things return to God, because even the weakest existence returns to Him, and judgments follow what is strongest in each thing.

Just as matter and the pit of nonexistence are the end of physical things considered only as bodies, and of people who reject nature's commands, Hell is the end of souls that reject God's moral and religious commands.

In contrast, wise and intellectual ends belong to the long upward path. Their starting points are mistaken ideas suited only to false arguments, empty hopes, and desires opposed to true rational aims. Here, “tyrant” means a specific power of desire or a particular craving. These goals move further into nonexistence as they become more limited and fade away, as we see when trivial aims of the past vanish. A wise person says, “How sorry I am for what I neglected in my duty to God.”

What happens to all happens to each one. As God says, “Your creation and your rising are only like the creation and rising of one soul.” After natural forms are complete, the first blowing brings them death and decay. A second blowing brings fear and collapse to the souls that have completed their development; it puts out their light. In the next blowing, their fire and greater light are kindled: the souls receive imaginal forms through God's breath. So one form dies and another lives. The author will explain this later.

This is the imaginal earth, lit by its Lord's light—the divine light that guides the soul. It is like many pieces of wood and wicks lit by a great fire. When the author says that this may mean the earth we know, he means any earth, simple or compound, including bodies. He says “after it has been taken into God's hand” because the verse appears in the context of Resurrection, after the blowing that brings death and before the books of deeds are placed and the prophets and witnesses are brought forward. The earth can also mean the fullest capacity to receive existence, and God's complete light and unity.
This interpretation leads to another, and the verses are connected in the chapter of The Groups. But the verse about God's hand comes before the others, so the commentator turns to explain it here.

We have already seen that only a weak trace like matter remains at the edge of the heavenly body's form. Its resistance to outside change comes from its soul, not its body. This supports the idea that the heavens are folded up.

The fire and other forms exist hidden within matter and then appear from it. Matter contains all forms only as possibilities; a form is what makes a thing actual, while matter is only what makes it possible.
This is the imaginal form that corresponds to the natural form.
This supports the author's claim that these forms have life in their own right.
In all five places, “this fire” means the soul-form. “The fire in the higher world” means the first, intellectual fire.

Up to the phrase “plants of the earth,” the philosopher gives examples that are not true as they sound and cannot be used as proof. If he means the compound earth, then it includes plant life and minerals, which may have an active inner form. But his goal is to prove an active form within the simple earth, even though earth should receive action rather than act. So words like “growth” and “sprouting” should mean the earth's cooling, drying, and holding forms together. The earth's inner soul-form guides these actions.

I must say that Ibn Arabi's insight is very deep, and deserves to be written in gold, not ink. “Life” can mean the source of perception and action, as when we say a living thing is aware and active. This is the life usually attributed to spirits. It belongs to spirits naturally, but to bodies only through something else. “Life” can also mean simple, all-pervading existence. We have often called this “the life that flows through everything.” In that sense, it belongs to all things that exist, including bodies. How could it not, when a body exists, and existence is life in each thing according to its level?

When great philosophers call bodies decaying, dead, or dark, they mean the first kind of life. It comes to bodies from spirits, so they have one life of their own and another received from outside. It is strange that the author says this here, when he repeatedly teaches in this book and elsewhere that life, knowledge, and will follow from existence or are the same as it. I have often shown this rule by looking at the rational soul: its existence is its knowledge of itself, its life, light, will, and love of itself. It is also its power to take on many states through its powers and images. For the author and other knowers, the soul is existence itself.

When Ibn Arabi says that stones and crafted vessels have forms of life, he means existence, though it is a passing existence received from another. His statement that bodies remember and praise God is also true. The author establishes this in his early discussion of general principles, and I have explained it in my notes. When we set aside the differences between things, their praise is included in God's own praise, as the verse says, “There is nothing that does not praise Him.” That is, each thing praises God through its own existence.

If “speech” means human speech, then animals do not have it either. But if it means each thing's own kind of speech, then everything speaks and is guided to what it was made for. Every existence is a word. Seen as coming from God, it is God's word; seen as belonging to its own nature, it is that nature's word. It describes God's qualities and displays His names. Praise describes the praised one's qualities and gifts, and the existence that flows through all things praises itself in this way.
Ibn Arabi's wording keeps the different levels in view, even if one level is only a shadow of a light or a branch of a source.
The verses about all things praising God show that existence, wherever it is, has life, knowledge, awareness, and will. Ibn Arabi himself says that God is with us wherever we are.

The author could say that bodies are dead and dark compared with the animal life that enables awareness and action. But they are not dead compared with the deeper life that belongs to existence and flows through all things. “We made every living thing from water” means that life arises from the life of existence. Even matter, which is lower than bodies, is alive in this sense because it exists. The author's statement that bodies are mixed with absence already shows that they have existence.

If relative death and darkness made them unable to be alive, aware, or praising in any sense, then they would also be dead in relation to the highest life: knowledge of God, His qualities, and His actions. People who know God would then be alive, while others were dead. How could the praise of all things show that all things have life? We do not deny the life and praise of imaginal bodies or other forms. But life has three levels: general, special, and most special, as we have explained.
This interpretation changes Ibn Arabi's meaning. He clearly says that life belongs to bodies in their own right, not that they receive it from outside.

The root meaning of “the Hour” may be “striving” or “moving quickly,” as some dictionaries suggest. One may explain the word by saying that “the Hour” comes from this root. The Qur'an uses it for the brief moment when the Resurrection begins, a short time in which a great event takes place. The author says the word also points to the fact that Resurrection is hidden within the world of nature and is part of the soul's long upward journey. This is why people see it at different distances: God says they think it is far away, while He sees it as near. It may be called a “day,” as in the verse that describes a day lasting fifty thousand years; it may be called an “hour”; or it may be even shorter, “like the blink of an eye, or shorter still.” The return to God is like the beginning of creation.

What happens to all happens to each one. As the verse says, “Your creation and your rising are only like the creation and rising of one soul.” Each soul reaches its end and becomes independent of the body and its powers. In the same way, all things move toward their ends and return to their source, until they reach the final end. The smaller hours are included in the Great Hour, but sense and imagination cannot grasp the whole of this movement. Even the intellect can know it only in a general way: everything moves toward its end through an endless chain of inner change. The time of one limited change is limited, but the time of endlessly many changes has no end. Compared with the Source of all sources, however, it is like the blink of an eye, or even shorter.

Light and forms may be imagined as a cone, with its point at the world beyond matter and its broad base at the material world—or the other way around. If we focus on simplicity and unity, the point belongs to the world beyond matter, where things are most simple and united, while the material world is divided and mixed. If we focus on the amount of existence, the world beyond matter is wider, and the material world is the narrow point.

This is a kind of metaphor used with verbs. For example, “the situation spoke” means that it showed or pointed to something. The Qur'an's phrase “they bought error in exchange for guidance” means that they chose error instead of guidance.

This comment corrects al-Razi's claim that the blowing does not happen twice. The first blowing causes death in the lower world; this matches Ibn Arabi's account of two blowings. The author then explains that the first ends natural forms and the second strengthens the link between spirits and simple imaginal forms. The first form dies; the second is used and brought to life.
A report says that a sound is made in the horn as many times as there are creatures. This points to the meaning just described.

“The eye” here means either the form itself and its inner reality, or the sight of that imaginal form. It can be called the “eye” because the senses in that world are joined; each sense does the work of all the others.

Rather, they are people of God. They are not subject to changing worlds or time, because they are not the spheres and bodies made of elements that come into being and pass away. In their inner reality, they are simple intellects and spirits sent free of place, time, and direction. Their home is the world of divine power; their time is the highest, rightward realm; their direction is a spiritual ascent through light. They rise like the angels who are near to God. A Persian poem says: “When I became empty of myself, I knew nothing but God. I disappeared from myself and remained through the Real; my garment of being was torn open at once.”

The great Resurrection belongs to an upward path through levels of being, not to a point on the ordinary timeline. That is why the Prophet was taught to answer questions about its timing by saying, “Its knowledge is with my Lord.” Anyone who tries to find its time by looking ahead along ordinary time is making the same mistake as someone who looks backward in time to find the eternal Source. It is like mistaking a swelling for something substantial. Thinkers find this difficult, let alone people who rely mainly on imagination. The author says that the Day of the great Resurrection is to the small resurrections of each breath as a day is to its hours, or a year to its days. Mawlana says, in effect: “Who would ask when the great Gathering will come, while it is already gathering all things?”

The signs of the great Resurrection have counterparts in the small one. When the earth shakes on that day, the body's ground shakes at death and its structure trembles. When the earth and mountains are lifted and crushed, the body's bones are crushed. When the stars are darkened, the lights of the body's powers go out. When the sun is folded up and the moon darkens, the spirit of the heart—the sun of the small world—comes to an end, and the light of the spirit in the brain, which depends on the heart, fades. When all creatures are gathered to God, the soul's many powers are gathered into one simple spiritual self.

This refers to God's fullest revelation of Himself through His names “the One,” “the Unique,” and “the All-Subduing.” Individual natures disappear, and all existence returns to God; the link between existence and separate natures falls away. Before the great Resurrection, beings appear as many and are linked to their individual natures. At the Resurrection, even separate intellects lose that distinction, because every trace of otherness is overcome. In this account, the natural world is the world of what is separate from God.
They exist in a fuller and brighter way, as explained earlier.

This upward return is a rise in the order of being, not movement through space. The soul rises as it is uncovered and freed from its coverings. The author says that the words “Resurrection” and “gathering” are fully fitting only when the soul is completely free of matter, as Ali said at that moment, “By the Lord of the Kaaba, I have won.” Yet the truth of Resurrection is already present. The Resurrection of ordinary people, whose goals and rewards still take bodily form, is not the same as the Resurrection of those who have reached the truth and attained the highest qualities they could receive from God. The author alludes to the end of Avicenna's The Healing, where the fully realized person is described as a human being shaped by divine qualities.
This means the soul of a heavenly sphere, which is like an image of imagination. The author says “power” because imagining and the power to imagine are one.
The scattered lights we see here will then become stronger, more unified lights of the spiritual world.
This is like the way the First Source appears to those who know it.

The author means especially good habits and beautiful forms. The “Garden of Qualities” and “Garden of the Essence” are familiar ideas to those who have trained themselves in good character and reached spiritual insight. Two Persian poems make the point:
Whoever has not seen the Beloved's face today is like a child on the road, still waiting for tomorrow.
They have put off our promised meeting until tomorrow; I hope tomorrow never comes between us.

This is like the state of certain saints, called the Abdal, whose shadowed being is said to have become luminous, along with their senses. One of them says, “I see only Your face and hear only Your voice.” Husayn ibn Ali says, “Blind is the eye that does not see You.”
This refers to people whose intermediate world remains inactive. May God protect us from that.
The problem comes from judging by outward appearances. The author cites a Persian poem:

Many have been led astray by outward form; they aimed at the form and missed God. For this reason the world has gone astray, and few know God's true friends. They say, “They are human, just like us; we all sleep and eat.” Do not judge the pure by yourself: a lion and milk may share the same written name, but they are not the same.

Every natural being worships through its created nature by obeying the commands and limits built into it. Human beings also have worship that comes through religious duties. Here, a soul's “condition” means its states, character, knowledge, and understanding. The religious motive is the intention to draw near to God. The human being is the traveler; the path is what moves within the traveler.

The perfect human being reflects the all-encompassing divine name, God. They may also reflect names such as the All-Hearing, the All-Seeing, the Knower, the Overpowering, the One who leads astray, or the One who lowers. But they are servants of God as a whole, not servants of only one of these names.

To stray from one's original nature may mean falling short of the highest rank without necessarily falling into Hell. This reading includes the people of the right, since God divides people into three groups: those brought near, those on the right, and those on the left.
The path has two lanes: one develops theoretical understanding, the other practical reason. The first is finer than a hair; the second sharper than a sword.

There are four stages: clearing and polishing, cleansing away, adorning, and passing beyond the self. The final act is witnessing God. At that stage, a person sees every kind of knowledge, power, quality, and existence as absorbed in God's knowing, power, and being.
These are people of high resolve who cut off their ties to the world all at once. A Persian verse says: “Take one step beyond yourself; the next lies in the Friend's lane.”

This applies if the goal is the garden of God's pure essence, in the light of that essence. Otherwise, the journey within God is itself the garden of His qualities. How, then, could there be a journey from God?
They do not possess the root; how could they possess the branch—the path that leads to it?
“Tyrants” here means the tyrants among them.
The seven groups may refer to the seven planets, the teachings of the seven prophets of resolve, or the seven subtle powers of the human being. God's outpouring and light never stop or fade.

They accepted Islam outwardly, through attachment, but did not live it fully. Islam means surrender and steadfastness, as in God's command, “Stand firm, as you have been commanded.” The bridge of mercy keeps them from being consumed by the fire of their nature before they have crossed.
These are people who sin openly, unlike those who keep their faults hidden.

People may fast to obey God, to clear the heart—for hunger is a cloud that rains wisdom—to understand the poor, or to take on the quality of the Self-Sufficient, who does not eat. People may give alms to obey, to develop generosity, to show compassion, or to take on the quality of the Provider, who meets needs. The light of an act depends on the intention behind it.
Other kinds of knowledge are tools, not ends in themselves. Good deeds polish the mirror of the heart. A sacred report says, “I created the creatures so that I might be known.”

The author brings together the path's two sides: theoretical understanding and practical action, each with its own stages. Though spiritual in its meaning, the path also has a visible form in the afterlife, like a bridge over a deep pit of Fire.

The three-branched shadow stands for the dark state of material nature. It is spread out in space, with length, width, and depth, and its parts are separated from one another. It cannot protect the soul from the fire of desire; nor can it escape the burning that comes from being spread out in time.
A traditional prayer addressed to the Imams calls them “the greatest path and the most upright way.”
The path, the traveler, the distance, and the movement are one. So too are the starting point of the movement and the point it reaches.

Movement here is cyclical: action follows knowledge, and knowledge is built on earlier action and knowledge. To put the foot on the head means acting according to the light of one's knowledge; to put the head on the foot means building new understanding on the results of one's knowledge, which itself rests on earlier understanding.

Knowledge is included among deeds, since it is an act of the heart. The record contains three kinds of forms: states and settled traits, which are both effects and sources of deeds; corresponding images that appear in the soul; and conscious representations of the deeds. Even now, despite all the veils and distractions, a person can look back and see their deeds imprinted in the book of the self. How much clearer will they be when the veil is lifted?

The agents that record different kinds of things include the Active Intellect for universal forms, souls embedded in matter, suspended images, divine forms, and subtle ties corresponding to individual things.
A good deed leads to another good deed until goodness becomes a settled trait.

Good traits form ranks of angels—beautiful youths and everlasting boys, or good influences and choices in this life. Every thought and action points toward more good. Lights descend on them from every side. A Persian verse says: “The light of lights, from right and left, / has cast a collar around my head and neck.” The same applies, in reverse, to darkness and the powers that display it.

Saying that the angel and devil have “one substance” points to the unity of what is named. Scripture also speaks of punishing angels. The angelic trait has a side that displays God's overpowering power.

These forms are like souls embedded in matter and like universal souls and intellects. They exist in a partial form at the lower level, and in a universal form at the higher level. The lower forms are held within the higher ones.
The three forms are the settled traits produced by deeds, the bodily images that represent them, and the conscious images of the deeds.

“The unbelieving devil” means the form of a trait created by repeated sin. Repeated sins may blacken the heart until a believer turns away from faith. The author also suggests that the perfect human being is the root from which the rest of creation branches, having been created from what remained of that person's clay. The human being's plant and animal powers are likewise roots from which plants and animals branch. The same applies to character: love and power in the perfect human are roots from which other forms of love and power branch. The same is true of the perfect human being's protection from error in knowledge and action, and of the corresponding qualities in angels.

One might object: if the human soul itself causes reward and punishment, how can God be the one who rewards and punishes, as scripture and the shared teaching of believers say? The answer is that God is the giver of all existence, light, and darkness. Nothing acts independently of Him. Intellects, souls, and powers are channels through which His action is specified. Whether existence appears through mercy or through power, it is God's outpouring, directly or through one or more intermediaries. The effects of the soul exist through God, but their particular forms are specified through the soul.

This is like a dream, which is called “the little death.” The sky above you, the ground beneath you, the person who speaks to you, and whatever pleases or hurts you are all objects of your knowledge. Knowledge that acts is the same as power.

The “bird” may mean the record of a person's deeds, which is the person themselves. It may also refer to their good or bad fortune. People often use a bird as a sign of what is to come, as in the expression “the crow of separation.”
The phrase points to the words “We will bring you into a form you do not know.” The implication comes from the verb “bring into being.”

The word “total” comes from an accountant's way of adding: “This is two, this is three, this is five; the total is ten.” Here, the total or summary means the settled traits, the separate entries are the repeated deeds and words of this life, and the book that counts them all is the human soul.

For those brought near to God, this is clear. They become simple, universal intellects and spirits free of matter, time, place, and other veils. All forms are gathered into their being. A report says that Ali recited the whole Qur'an at once, meaning the Qur'an in every sense: written or created, in the world or within the self. This all-encompassing awareness is a lasting rank for those brought near.

Those on the right have not completed their theoretical understanding, and those on the left have not done so either. For them, seeing everything in one moment is not a lasting rank; their spiritual freedom is only partial and temporary. They have simple awareness, not awareness that reflects on itself. The state of those brought near is like that of people continually absorbed in Joseph's beauty; the state of those on the right and left is like that of the women who were struck by his beauty for a time. A settled trait is itself a simple state that contains the actions flowing from it. To see that trait is to see all those actions at once.

There is a difficulty about bodily resurrection. Scripture and tradition describe changes and successive events in the afterlife: skins are replaced, and the people of Paradise eat, drink, move, and enjoy one another in sequence. The same applies, in a way suited to them, to the people of Hell. Yet potentiality and material matter belong to this world, not the next. This world is the field of sowing; the next is the harvest. If so, all that follows from a person's deeds and traits should appear at once. This seems to support the idea that everyone sees everything in a single instant. But neither reason nor revelation supports that as a general rank, and many philosophers who deny that separate things can be known by immaterial beings cannot explain it. How could it apply to those on the right, let alone those on the left? If it did, they would all have the highest rank, though they lack the knowledge and standing required for it. God's acts are not arbitrary. The claim makes sense for the active intellect and universal intellects, but the difficulty does not concern them.

The truth is that afterlife forms are pure images, with extension but no material bearer. They depend on God for their existence. Their parts cannot occupy the same place or moment, not because matter prevents them, but because this belongs to their own nature. In this world, too, extended parts cannot occupy the same place, and successive moments cannot occur together. This explains the forms perceived. As for the one who perceives them, even someone on the right has not brought their theoretical intellect—which gives true spiritual freedom and breadth—from potentiality into full activity. Their existence is therefore still limited in its second nature. The rational soul is subtle, but it takes the form of what it turns toward. Having spent its life joined to extended images and passing particulars, it follows their pattern: it experiences its desires, meals, and other pleasures one after another. It does not have endlessly many meals or encounters, but it may have many, one after another. This is how the author resolves the difficulty.
We learn sound logic by joining with the Active Intellect and by following God's messengers. Logic is the measure of the sciences.

“The balance” here means the general measure that includes the five kinds. The author's answer shows that the Qur'an contains a measure of knowledge; the separate question of where it uses each of the five kinds is answered in detail in The Keys to the Unseen.

Philosophers commonly call Aristotle the First Teacher, since he established logic, and al-Farabi the Second Teacher, since he brought it from Greek into Arabic. The author instead says that God is the first teacher, Gabriel the second, and the Messenger the third. This is the inward chain of teaching through spiritual beings; outwardly, the teaching comes through receiving the Qur'an.

The three forms of the measure of equality are the first, second, and third figures of the syllogism. The author does not count a fourth, since it is less natural. The measure of entailment is the conditional syllogism; the measure of contradiction is the disjunctive syllogism. He gives Qur'anic examples of each. For example, “He is the One who begins creation, then brings it back, and that is easier for Him” compares the easier return with the first creation. “I do not declare myself innocent; the soul urges one to evil” reasons from the soul to a general rule. Abraham says of a setting star, “I do not love those that set,” contrasting it with his Lord, who does not set. Another passage reasons that God is not rightly understood by those who say He revealed nothing to any human, since Moses was human and received a revealed Book. The conditional form appears in “If there were other gods in heaven and earth besides God, both would be ruined”; the disjunctive form in “Either we or you are rightly guided, or plainly in error.” The author notes that scripture and religious law use many concepts without their formal technical names. Their presence in the Qur'an does not make them innovations. He asks God to grant fairness and protect people from injustice.

The author's comparison is polemical. He says that Hanbalites and others rely only on the senses, imagination, and estimation, while a pure philosopher relies only on reason. These would be like the senses and reason within one human being if each were active on its own. Neither side alone is complete. The people who bring the faculties together are, in the author's view, the successful, rightly guided, and glad.
A person should compare the two worlds by using sound reason and accept that every natural form in this world has a corresponding imaginal form in the next.
This refers to those who interpret Qur'anic passages about the beginning and the return as referring only to spirits and abstract meanings. For them, “form” refers only to material forms.
This is the world of intellects that exist through God's sustaining power. It contains pure meanings, with no attachment or form—neither an imaginal form nor a natural one.

The scales of knowledge are heavy when there is more to weigh by the five measures, especially when the measure is demonstrative proof. The scales of deeds are heavy when the pan of good deeds outweighs the pan of bad deeds. The author is not speaking loosely about “heavy” and “light.”

Those on the spiritual path also take account of themselves, watch over their actions, and weigh their good and bad deeds each night. If their bad deeds outweigh the good, they make up for them through repentance, returning to God, remembrance, and worship. If the two sides are equal, they add night worship to tip the balance toward good. If their good deeds outweigh the bad, they compare them with God's countless blessings, both outward and inward, and return in humility, asking forgiveness and protection through His generosity. If they reflect, they will see that even their acts of worship came through God's help and guidance, and are among His greatest gifts. God says, “Do not claim that you have done God a favor by accepting Islam. Rather, God has favored you by guiding you to faith.”

The full verse says: “Do not drive away those who call on their Lord morning and evening, seeking His face. You are not responsible for their account, nor are they responsible for yours; if you drive them away, you will be among the wrongdoers.”
The word translated “unjust” can also mean “one counted among the unjust,” as in words for a blacksmith, date seller, or grocer.

“Powers that act” does not mean the intellects called the lords of species, since they too pass away. It means the beautiful names of God, which mystics see as the powers that nurture things. The visible forms disappear into the One who appears through them, just as animals return to the names “All-Hearing,” “All-Seeing,” and “All-Knowing,” angels to “All-Pure” and “All-Holy,” and the human being to the name God.

This means that all natural forms change, along the full course of their development, into forms of the intermediate world. Those forms belong to the level of souls, just as souls belong to the level of intellects. The universal divine souls are, in this account, the same as the intellects. All the goals of natural things are contained in the highest goal, whose unity is a true oneness, not a count of separate things. All things stand there through God, the Sustainer, not through material receivers. This change is not only a change in how someone looks at things when they set aside ordinary relationships. Reaching that view can itself be a spiritual station while a person is alive, and a necessary step toward the highest goal. “Whoever is blind here will be blind in the next life.” Knowledge is the seed of seeing.
This means that God owns everything, because everything there exists through His existence. This is the meaning of the verse, “Suddenly they will all be standing, looking on.”
